title: So Let the Calamity Be Great and the Matter Grievous
intro: Abu Tammam wrote this elegy for Muhammad ibn Humayd al-Tusi, one of the caliph al-Ma'mun's generals, sent against the Khurramite rebel Babak; al-Tabari records that Babak killed him at Hashtadsar in 214 AH (829 CE), and Ibn al-Athir that when Babak's ambush broke his army in the mountains he held his ground until all but one of his men had fled, then, riding off with that one to save himself, came on the Khurramites fighting a band of his soldiers and made for them; drawn by his fine bearing, they fought him until a javelin brought down his horse and he was killed. The poem opens by magnifying the calamity and blaming any eye that does not weep, praises his generosity, follows him to a martyr's death, mourns him with his clan of Nabhan of Tayyi' and the tribes beyond, and ends by blessing his grave and bidding him God's peace. Al-Suli tells how the prince Abu Dulaf recited some of its lines and said to the poet, “By God, I wish you had said this about me,” and then, “Whoever is mourned with poetry like this has not died.” Ibn Ammar, in an epistle on Abu Tammam's errors, called it “the mother of his necklaces”, the poem that made his name, and attacked its opening and several of its words; he also passed on Di'bil's claim that the poet had lifted lines from an elegy by Abu Sulma al-Muzani, which al-Hasan ibn Wahb, al-Suli reports, rejected: he knew that elegy, it shared nothing with Abu Tammam's, and Di'bil had merged the two, both elegies in one metre, to slander him.

translation: So let the calamity be great, the matter grievous:
no eye that has not overflowed has an excuse.
1.sharh: Let a calamity be as great as this one: no dry eye has an excuse. Critics said the opening points to a loss not yet named, in words fit only for joy; al-Suli answered that the Quran itself gives “good tidings” of punishment (3:21).

translation: Hope died after Muhammad,
and travellers are too busy now for travel.
2.sharh: With Muhammad dead, hope died too: those who set out in search of his gifts have no one left to travel to. The commentators are silent here. The last two words differ only by a vowel.

translation: He was the wealth of every man whose wealth was small,
the savings of whoever was left with no savings.
3.sharh: He gave so freely that the poor lived on his money as if it were theirs, and those with nothing put by could count on him as on a hoard. Each half ends by repeating its key word: wealth, then savings.

translation: Whoever came seeking his hand's bounty never knew,
when it poured, that hardship had ever been made.
4.sharh: His hand poured out gifts like rain, so that those who came asking never learned that want existed. The verb is used of the first downpour of a storm, which turns the hand into a raincloud.

translation: It was in God's cause that he died, the man for whom
the roads of God's cause stand idle, and the frontier gapes.
5.sharh: He died fighting for the faith, and with him gone no one rides out on holy war and the border lies open to the enemy. Ibn Ammar objected that Arabs say iththaghara, not inthaghara, for “gaped”.

translation: A man for whom, whenever a tribe's eyes overflowed
with blood, the stories and the fame told of him smiled.
6.sharh: Whenever a tribe wept blood for the men he had killed, his name shone the brighter. The commentators are silent; it may also mean that tribes wept blood for him while his memory smiled. Weeping is set against laughter.

translation: A man who died among sword-strokes and spear-thrusts, a death
that stood in for victory when victory escaped him.
7.sharh: He fell fighting, and his death stood in for the victory he did not live to win: a martyr lives on with God, says al-Kharzanji; dying face to the enemy was enough, says Abu Yahya; for al-Suli, others' later victory counts as his.

translation: He did not die until the edge of his sword had died
of striking, and the brown spears had fallen sick on him.
8.sharh: He fought until his blade was too notched to cut and his spears too splintered to thrust, Abu Yahya explains, and only then died, so no one can blame him. The sword is given a death, the spears an illness.

translation: Escaping death had been easy, but he was turned back to it
by a bitter sense of honour and a rugged nature.
9.sharh: He could have fled and lived, but honour and a temper hard on his enemies sent him back. Al-Amidi traces the idea to Abd Yaghuth's “had I wished, a sturdy mare would have saved me”, but judges Abu Tammam's lines the better.

translation: And by a soul that loathes disgrace, as if disgrace
on the day of terror were unbelief, or unbelief less.
10.sharh: A third thing sent him back: a spirit to which running away in battle was as bad as renouncing the faith, or worse. “A soul” is the third subject of “turned back” in the line before.

translation: He planted his foot in the pool where death collects
and told it: “From under your sole is the Gathering.”
11.sharh: He stood where the killing was thickest and bade his foot stay, for it would rise from that spot at the Resurrection. Ibn Ammar said no Arab or poet speaks so; al-Amidi called lines 7 to 11 “the utmost in beauty and sweetness”.

translation: He went out at dawn, his cloak woven of praise,
and left the field only with reward for his shroud.
12.sharh: He rode out in the morning clothed in men's praise and did not leave the battle alive; God's reward was his shroud. The cloak of setting out answers the shroud, praise in this world reward in the next.

translation: He put on death's garments red, and night
had not come upon them before they were green silk.
13.sharh: His clothes were red with his blood, and before nightfall they had become the green silk of paradise, where martyrs are clothed, says Abu Yahya. Rhetoricians cite it for its colours: red for being killed, green for paradise.

translation: On the day he died the sons of Nabhan were like
the stars of a sky from among which the full moon fell.
14.sharh: His clan were stars and he their full moon: they still shine, but less brightly. Critics heard an insult to his clan; al-Suli answers with Jarir's elegy for the caliph al-Walid, whose sons were “like the stars from among which the moon has fallen”.

translation: They are consoled for a man the heights themselves are consoled for;
generosity, valour and poetry weep for him.
15.sharh: His clan receives condolences, but glory itself is bereaved, and every virtue he had mourns him; he left no successor in any, says Abu Yahya. The poetry, says Ibn al-Mustawfi, is verse about him, not by him.

translation: How could they bear his loss patiently, when he went on
into death until he and patience were martyred together?
16.sharh: His people cannot be patient over him: he advanced into death so steadfastly that patience itself fell a martyr beside him. Once he was killed, says al-Kharzanji, no patience was left to anyone.

translation: A man gentle of spirit, not from any meekness,
but from too much pride to have pride said of him.
17.sharh: His mildness came not from weakness but from disdain for arrogance: he was too proud to be thought proud. Abu al-Ala' reads “pride” either as the subject of “but”, its predicate unsaid, or as the reason: “out of pride”.

translation: A man the horses robbed, though he was their shield;
the fire of war stripped him, though he was its embers.
18.sharh: The cavalry he protected carried him off, and the war he kept burning consumed him. Abu al-Ala' explains that one rider killed him, as a people is said to kill a man when one of them did it.

translation: The white swords with their damask grain were keen
in battle; now, after him, they are cut short.
19.sharh: The swords that cut so well are useless now, al-Suli says, since no one wields them as he did. Abu al-Ala' adds that butr, “cut short”, also means left without heirs, as in the Quran (108:3): the swords are childless.

translation: Now that misfortune has folded Muhammad away,
will the robes of generosity ever be unfolded again?
20.sharh: Death has folded Muhammad up like a garment, and generosity, which was his clothing, will never be spread out again. The question expects the answer no; folding is set against unfolding.

translation: When the trees of kindness are cut down at the root,
on what branch will fresh leaves be found?
21.sharh: He was the root of all kindness, and with the root cut no branch can put out green leaves. Abu Yahya: he was a trunk that was felled, with no shoot left behind.

translation: If Tayyi' has been dressed in the calamity of his loss,
Tamim and Bakr have not been left bare of it.
22.sharh: His death is not his own tribe's grief alone: Tayyi' wears it like a garment, and the great tribes of Tamim and Bakr have their share too. Being dressed is set against being left bare.

translation: So it is: we never cease to lose a man
whose loss the desert and the town share with us.
23.sharh: Such is the lot of his tribe, which is the poet's own: the men it loses are mourned by nomads and townsmen alike. The commentators are silent; al-Suli's edition reads “she never ceases to lose”, which may make Tayyi' the subject.

translation: May rain water a rain whose body the earth now hides,
though it had neither clouds nor drops.
24.sharh: He prays for rain on the grave, then calls the dead man himself a rain, for his giving was the rain people lived on, though he had no cloud and shed no water. The commentators are silent.

translation: And how could I take it as a favour from the clouds
to water a grave when the sea lies in its niche?
25.sharh: He takes his prayer back: the clouds can do the dead man no favour by watering his grave, since the sea of his generosity lies inside it. The commentators are silent on this line and the one before.

translation: He left this world clean-robed; the morning he was laid to rest
there was no garden that did not wish to be his grave.
26.sharh: He died with a spotless name, and every garden longed to hold him. Some copies read “no plot of ground” for “no garden”, and Ibn Ammar called that the worst word that could have been put there.

translation: He dwells in the earth now, he by whom the earth had life,
whose lavish giving used to drown the blows of fate.
27.sharh: The man whose gifts kept the land green and drowned every misfortune now lies in that land; the soil grew moist with his bounty, says Abu Yahya. Thawa and thara, yaghmur and ghamr echo across the halves.

translation: God's peace be on you, endowed for ever, for I have seen
that the noble, free-born man is granted no long life.
28.sharh: He wishes God's peace on the dead man for ever, and consoles himself that men of his worth are never given long lives. One manuscript has “no excuse” for “no life”, a misreading according to al-Suli's editor.

1.1.3.head: الخَطب
1.1.3.meaning: Khatb: a matter of weight; here, a calamity.

1.2.4.head: فاضَ
1.2.4.meaning: Overflow with tears. Al-Suli's edition prints yaghid, “sink away”: an eye that has not wept itself dry.

2.1.4.head: مُحَمَّد
2.1.4.meaning: Muhammad ibn Humayd al-Tusi, one of al-Ma'mun's generals, killed fighting Babak the Khurramite in 214 AH (829 CE).

4.1.4.meaning: Mujtadi: one who comes seeking a gift (jadwa).

5.2.5.head: الثَّغر
5.2.5.meaning: Thaghr: a frontier post facing enemy land; literally a gap or opening.

6.2.2-3.meaning: “Smiled about him”: laughter stands for joy and brightness.

8.1.5.head: مَضرِب
8.1.5.meaning: Madrib: the part of the blade that strikes, its cutting edge.

8.2.5-6.meaning: “The brown spears”: spears, named for the colour of their shafts.

9.2.2.head: الحِفاظ
9.2.2.meaning: Hifaz: fierce defence of what one is bound to protect, in war above all.

11.1.3-4.meaning: “The pool of death”: the place where death collects, as water pools.

11.2.5.head: أَخمَص
11.2.5.meaning: Akhmas: the hollow of the sole that does not touch the ground.

11.2.6.head: الحَشر
11.2.6.meaning: Hashr: the gathering of the dead on the Day of Judgement.

12.1.5.head: رِداء
12.1.5.meaning: Rida': a cloak worn over the shoulders.

13.2.6.head: سُندُس
13.2.6.meaning: Sundus: fine silk; the Quran clothes the people of paradise in “garments of green sundus” (76:21).

14.1.2-3.meaning: Banu Nabhan: a clan of the tribe of Tayyi', the dead man's people.

15.1.3.meaning: Thawi: one who stays; here, the dead man in his grave.

15.2.4.head: البَأس
15.2.4.meaning: Ba's: courage and strength in war.

18.1.5.head: حِمى
18.1.5.meaning: Hima: protection; he was their guard. Abu al-Ala' reads “their beauty”.

18.2.1.head: بَزَّ
18.2.1.meaning: Stripped him, took him by force.

19.1.3.head: البيض
19.1.3.meaning: “The white ones”: swords, called white for their gleam.

19.1.4.head: المَآثير
19.1.4.meaning: Ma'athir: swords whose steel shows the watered pattern of damask (athar).

21.1.3.head: العُرف
21.1.3.meaning: Urf: kindness, good done to others.

22.1.5.head: طَيِّئ
22.1.5.meaning: Tayyi': an Arab tribe of Yemeni origin, the tribe of the dead man and of the poet.

22.2.4.head: تَميم
22.2.4.meaning: Tamim: a great Arab tribe, the sons of Tamim ibn Murr.

22.2.6.head: بَكر
22.2.6.meaning: Bakr: a great Arab tribe, the sons of Bakr ibn Wa'il.

23.2.4-5.meaning: “The desert and the town”: nomads and settled people, everyone.

25.2.4.head: لَحد
25.2.4.meaning: Lahd: the niche cut in the side of a grave, where the body is laid.

27.2.2-3.meaning: “The turns of fate”: misfortunes, the blows of time.

28.1.4.head: وَقف
28.1.4.meaning: Waqf: an endowment; here, God's peace held for him in perpetuity, as land is given to the poor for ever.
